title: Part 6, Chapter 8
paragraphs: When he entered Sonia's room, it was already growing dark. Sonia had been waiting for him all day in terrible anxiety. Dounia had been waiting with her. She had come that morning, remembering Svidrigailov's words that Sonia knew. We will not describe the conversation and tears of the two women, or how quickly they became friends. From that meeting Dounia drew at least one comfort: her brother would not be alone. He had gone to Sonia first with his confession; he had come to her for human connection when he needed it most. Sonia would follow him wherever fate might send him. Dounia did not need to ask -- she knew. She looked at Sonia almost with reverence, which at first nearly embarrassed the girl. Sonia felt herself, on the contrary, hardly worthy of looking at Dounia. The gracious image of Dounia bowing to her so attentively and respectfully at their first meeting in Raskolnikov's room had remained in Sonia's mind as one of the most beautiful visions of her life.

Dounia eventually grew impatient and, leaving Sonia, went to her brother's room to wait for him there. She kept thinking he would come there first. After she left, Sonia was seized by the dread that he might kill himself. Dounia feared the same thing. But all day they had tried to reassure each other that it was impossible, and both were less anxious while together. The moment they parted, each could think of nothing else. Sonia remembered how Svidrigailov had told her the day before that Raskolnikov had two choices -- Siberia or... Besides, she knew his vanity, his pride, his lack of faith.
"Is it possible that only cowardice and fear of death keep him alive?" she wondered in despair.

Meanwhile the sun was setting. Sonia stood by the window, staring out dejectedly, but from her window she could see nothing but the unwhitewashed blank wall of the neighboring building. At last, when she had become nearly certain he was dead -- he walked into the room.
She cried out in joy, but looking carefully into his face, she turned pale.
"Yes," said Raskolnikov, smiling. "I've come for your cross, Sonia. It was you who told me to go to the crossroads. So why are you frightened now that the time has come?"

Sonia stared at him in astonishment. His tone struck her as strange; a cold shiver ran through her, but in an instant she understood that both the tone and the words were a mask. He spoke to her looking away, as though trying to avoid her eyes.

"You see, Sonia, I've decided it will be better this way. There's one particular fact... But it's a long story and there's no point discussing it. Do you know what infuriates me, though? It's that all those stupid, brutish faces will be gaping at me any minute now, bombarding me with their stupid questions, which I'll have to answer -- they'll point their fingers at me... No, I'm not going to Porfiry. I'm sick of him. I'd rather go to my friend, the Explosive Lieutenant -- what a sensation I'll cause! But I need to be calmer; I've become too irritable lately. Can you believe it -- I nearly shook my fist at my sister just now, because she turned around for one last look at me. What a brutal state I'm in! Well then, where are the crosses?"
He seemed barely aware of what he was doing. He couldn't stay still or concentrate his thoughts on anything; his mind raced from one thing to the next; his hands trembled slightly.
Without a word, Sonia took two crosses from the drawer -- one of cypress wood, one of copper. She made the sign of the cross over herself and over him, and hung the wooden cross around his neck.

"It's the symbol of my taking up the cross," he laughed. "As though I haven't suffered enough already! The wooden cross -- the peasant one; the copper one, Lizaveta's -- you'll wear it yourself. Show me! So she wore it... at that moment? I remember two things like these too -- a silver cross and a small icon. I threw them back on the old woman's chest. Those are the ones I should really be wearing now... But I'm talking nonsense and forgetting what matters; I keep losing my train of thought... You see, I came to warn you, Sonia, so you'd know... That's all -- that's all I came for. But I thought I had more to say. You wanted me to go yourself. Well, now I'm going to prison and you'll have your wish. So why are you crying? You too? Don't, stop it! Oh, how I hate all this!"

But his feelings were stirred; his heart ached as he looked at her. "Why is she suffering too?" he thought. "What am I to her? Why does she weep? Why does she look after me, like my mother, like Dounia? She'll end up being my nursemaid."
"Cross yourself. Say at least one prayer," Sonia begged in a timid, broken voice.
"Oh, certainly -- as many as you like! And sincerely, Sonia, sincerely..."
But he wanted to say something entirely different.

He crossed himself several times. Sonia picked up her shawl and draped it over her head. It was the green drap de dames shawl that Marmeladov had once described -- "the family shawl." Raskolnikov remembered and thought of it, but did not ask. He was becoming aware that he was hopelessly distracted and hideously agitated. This frightened him. He was also suddenly struck by the realization that Sonia intended to go with him.

"What are you doing? Where are you going? Stay here, stay! I'll go alone," he cried in cowardly irritation, almost resentful, and moved toward the door. "What's the point of making a procession of it?" he muttered as he went out.
Sonia remained standing in the middle of the room. He hadn't even said goodbye to her; he had already forgotten her. A sharp, rebellious doubt surged through his heart.
"Was this right? Was any of this right?" he thought again as he descended the stairs. "Couldn't he stop and take it all back... and not go?"

But he kept going. He felt suddenly, with absolute finality, that he must stop asking himself questions. Turning into the street, he remembered that he hadn't said goodbye to Sonia, that he had left her standing in the middle of the room in her green shawl, not daring to move after he had shouted at her. He stopped for a moment. In that same instant, another thought hit him, as though it had been lying in wait.

"Why did I go to her just now? I told her it was on business -- what business? I had no business! To tell her I was going? But where was the need? Do I love her? No -- no, I drove her away just now like a dog. Did I really want her crosses? Oh, how low I've sunk! No -- I wanted her tears, I wanted to see her terror, to watch her heart break! I needed something to cling to, something to delay me, a kind face to look at! And I dared to believe in myself, to dream of what I'd become! I'm a pathetic, contemptible wretch -- contemptible!"
He walked along the canal embankment. He didn't have much further to go. But at the bridge he stopped, turned off his path, and walked along it toward the Haymarket.

He looked eagerly left and right, gazing intently at every object, but unable to fix his attention on anything; everything slipped away. "In a week, a month, I'll be crossing this bridge in a prison van. How will I look at the canal then? I should try to remember this," slipped through his mind. "Look at that sign -- how will I read those letters then? It says 'Company' -- there, I should remember that letter 'a,' and look at it again in a month -- how will I see it then? What will I be feeling and thinking then? Good God, how trivial all this must be, what I'm fretting over now! Of course it must all be interesting in its way... Ha-ha-ha! What am I thinking? I'm turning into a child, showing off to myself. Why am I ashamed? Oh! -- that fat man who just shoved me -- a German, must be -- does he have any idea who he just pushed? There's a woman with a baby, begging. It's funny that she considers me more fortunate than herself. I should give her something, just for the absurdity of it. Here's a five-kopeck piece still in my pocket -- where did I get it? Here, here... take it, my good woman!"
"God bless you," the beggar chanted in a tearful voice.

He entered the Haymarket. It was distasteful, deeply distasteful, to be in a crowd, but he walked toward the thickest part of it. He would have given anything to be alone; but he knew that he couldn't have borne being alone for a single moment. A drunk was making a spectacle of himself, trying to dance and falling over. A ring of people had gathered around him. Raskolnikov pushed through the crowd, watched the drunk for several minutes, and gave a short, barking laugh. A minute later he had forgotten the man entirely and no longer saw him, though he was still staring. He drifted on, not remembering where he was, but when he reached the middle of the square, a sudden wave of feeling swept over him, overwhelming him body and soul.

He suddenly recalled Sonia's words: "Go to the crossroads, bow down to the people, kiss the earth -- for you have sinned against it too -- and say aloud to the whole world: 'I am a murderer.'" He trembled as he remembered. The hopeless misery and anxiety of all that time, especially the last hours, had weighed on him so heavily that he clutched at the chance for this new, pure, complete sensation. It came over him like a seizure; a single spark kindled in his soul and spread like fire. Everything in him softened at once, and tears sprang to his eyes. He fell to the earth where he stood...
He knelt in the middle of the square, bowed down to the ground, and kissed the filthy earth with bliss and rapture. He rose and bowed down a second time.
"That one's been drinking," a young man nearby observed.
There was a roar of laughter.

"He's going to Jerusalem, brothers, saying goodbye to his children and his homeland. He's bowing down to all the world and kissing the great city of Saint Petersburg and its pavement," added a slightly drunk workman.
"He's young, too!" someone else noted.
"And a gentleman," someone said in a more serious tone.
"Hard to tell who's a gentleman and who isn't these days."

These remarks and the laughter held Raskolnikov in check, and the words "I am a murderer," which had perhaps been on the tip of his tongue, died away. He endured the comments calmly, however, and without looking back, turned down a street leading toward the police station. Along the way he caught a glimpse of something that did not surprise him -- he had felt it must be so. The second time he had bowed down in the Haymarket, he had spotted Sonia about fifty paces away on his left, hiding behind one of the wooden market stalls. She had followed him on his agonizing journey! In that moment, Raskolnikov felt and knew once and for all that Sonia was with him forever and would follow him to the ends of the earth, wherever fate might take him. His heart was wrung... but he was already approaching the fatal place.

He entered the courtyard with a certain resolve. He had to climb to the third floor. "It'll take me a while to get up there," he thought. The decisive moment still seemed far off, as though he had plenty of time left to reconsider.

The same garbage, the same eggshells on the spiral staircase, the same open apartment doors, the same kitchens belching the same fumes and stench. Raskolnikov had not been here since that day. His legs were numb and buckling under him, but they kept moving forward. He stopped for a moment to catch his breath, to compose himself, to enter like a man. "But why? What for?" he asked himself. "If I must drain this cup, what difference does it make? The more repulsive, the better." He pictured the figure of the "Explosive Lieutenant," Ilya Petrovitch. Was he really going to him? Couldn't he go to someone else? To Nikodim Fomitch? Couldn't he turn around and go straight to Nikodim Fomitch's home? At least it would be done in private... No, no! To the Explosive Lieutenant! If he must drink the cup, drink it down at once.

Feeling cold and barely conscious, he opened the door to the police station. This time there were very few people inside -- just a building porter and a peasant. The doorkeeper didn't even glance out from behind his partition. Raskolnikov walked into the next room. "Maybe I still won't have to say anything," flashed through his mind. A clerk of some sort, not in uniform, was settling in at a desk to write. Another clerk was sitting down in the corner. Zametov was not there. Neither, of course, was Nikodim Fomitch.
"No one in?" Raskolnikov asked, addressing the man at the desk.
"Who are you looking for?"
"Well, well! Not a sound was heard, not a sight was seen, but I smell a Russian... how does that fairy tale go? I've forgotten! At your service!" a familiar voice suddenly cried.
Raskolnikov shuddered. The Explosive Lieutenant stood before him. He had just come in from the third room. "It's the hand of fate," thought Raskolnikov. "Why is he here?"

"Come to see us? What about?" Ilya Petrovitch cried. He was obviously in an excellent mood and perhaps slightly tipsy. "If it's on business, you're a bit early. It's only by chance that I'm here. But I'll do what I can. I must say, I... what is it, what is it? Forgive me..."

The translator's note read: Dostoevsky appears to have forgotten that it is after sunset, and that the last time Raskolnikov visited the police office at two in the afternoon he was reproached for coming too late.
"Raskolnikov."
"Of course -- Raskolnikov. You didn't think I'd forgotten? Don't think me that sort of man... Rodion Ro -- Ro -- Rodionovitch, that's it, isn't it?"
"Rodion Romanovitch."

"Yes, yes, of course, Rodion Romanovitch! I was just getting to it. I've made many inquiries about you. I assure you I've been genuinely sorry since that... since I behaved so badly... It was explained to me afterward that you were a literary man... a scholar of sorts. Mercy me! What literary or scientific man hasn't begun with some eccentricity? My wife and I have the deepest respect for literature -- my wife is a genuine devotee! Literature and art! As long as a man is a gentleman, everything else can be gained through talent, learning, good sense, genius. A hat -- well, what does a hat matter? I can buy a hat as easily as a bun. But what's under the hat, what the hat covers -- that I can't buy! I even meant to come and apologize to you, but I thought maybe... Anyway, is there something you need? I hear your family has arrived?"
"Yes, my mother and sister."

"I've even had the honor and pleasure of meeting your sister -- a highly cultured and charming person. I confess I was sorry about getting so heated with you that time. There it is! And as for my being suspicious about your fainting spell -- that's been thoroughly cleared up! Fanaticism and overwrought nerves! I understand your indignation perfectly. Perhaps you're changing lodgings now that your family has come?"
"No, I just dropped in... I came to ask... I thought I'd find Zametov here."

"Oh yes! Of course -- you two became friends, I heard. Well, no, Zametov is gone. Yes, we've lost Zametov. He left yesterday... quarreled with everybody on the way out, in the rudest way. He's a featherbrained young fool, nothing more; one might have expected something from him, but there -- you know how our brilliant young men are. He wanted to sit for some examination, but it's all just talk and boasting with him -- it never goes anywhere. Of course, it's a very different matter with you, or with your friend Mr. Razumihin. Yours is an intellectual career, and failure won't stop you. For you, one might say, all the pleasures of life amount to nothing -- you are an ascetic, a monk, a hermit! A book, a pen behind your ear, a scholarly paper -- that's where your spirit soars! I'm the same way myself... Have you read Livingstone's Travels?"
"No."
"I have. There are a great many nihilists about nowadays, you know, and it's not surprising, given the times. But we thought... you're not a nihilist, of course? Answer me frankly, frankly!"

"Believe me, you can speak as openly with me as you would with yourself! Official duty is one thing, but... You think I meant to say friendship is something else? No, you're wrong! It's not friendship I mean, but the feeling of a man and a citizen, the feeling of humanity and love for the Almighty. I may be an official, but I must always feel myself a man and a citizen. You were asking about Zametov. Zametov will get himself into some sordid scandal in a house of ill repute, with champagne flying -- that's the sum total of your Zametov! While I, perhaps, am burning with devotion and lofty feelings. Besides, I have rank, position, standing! I am married, have children, fulfill my duties as a man and a citizen. And who is he, may I ask? I appeal to you as a man ennobled by education... Then these midwives have become astonishingly common, too."

Raskolnikov raised his eyebrows. The words of Ilya Petrovitch, who had obviously been at dinner, were mostly a stream of empty sounds to him. But some of them he caught. He looked at the lieutenant inquiringly, not knowing where this was going.

"I mean those short-haired females," the talkative Ilya Petrovitch continued. "'Midwives' is my term for them. I think it's a fine one, ha-ha! They go to the medical academy, study anatomy. If I fall sick, am I supposed to send for some young lady to treat me? Ha-ha!" Ilya Petrovitch laughed, pleased with his own wit. "It's an immoderate passion for education, but once you're educated, enough is enough. Why abuse it? Why insult decent people, as that scoundrel Zametov does? And why did he insult me, I ask you? Then look at these suicides -- how common they've become, you can't imagine! People spend their last kopeck and kill themselves. Boys and girls, old men. Just this morning we heard about a gentleman newly arrived in town. Nil Pavlitch -- I say -- what was the name of that gentleman who shot himself?"
"Svidrigailov," someone answered from the other room, in a drowsy, listless voice.
Raskolnikov started.
"Svidrigailov! Svidrigailov shot himself!" he cried.
"What -- you knew Svidrigailov?"
"Yes... I knew him. He hadn't been in town long."

"That's right. He'd recently lost his wife, was a man of reckless habits, and suddenly shot himself -- in the most shocking way. He left a few words in his notebook saying he was dying in full possession of his faculties and that no one was to blame for his death. He had money, they say. How did you come to know him?"
"I... was acquainted with him. My sister was a governess in his family."
"Well, well, well! Then perhaps you can tell us something about him. You had no suspicion?"
"I saw him yesterday. He was... drinking wine. I knew nothing."
Raskolnikov felt as though something had fallen on him and was suffocating him.
"You've gone pale again. It's so stuffy in here..."
"Yes, I should go," Raskolnikov muttered. "Excuse me for troubling you..."
"Not at all! Come as often as you like. It's a pleasure, and I'm glad to say so."
Ilya Petrovitch held out his hand.
"I only wanted... I came to see Zametov."
"I understand, I understand. And it's a pleasure to see you."
"I... am very glad... goodbye," Raskolnikov smiled.

He went out. He was reeling, overcome by dizziness, barely conscious of what he was doing. He started down the stairs, bracing himself with his right hand against the wall. He was vaguely aware of a porter pushing past him on the way up to the station, of a dog barking shrilly on a lower floor, of a woman hurling a rolling pin at it and shouting. He made his way down and out into the courtyard. There, not far from the entrance, stood Sonia, deathly pale and stricken with horror. She looked at him wildly. He stopped before her. There was a look of poignant agony, of despair, on her face. She clasped her hands. An ugly, meaningless smile twisted his lips. He stood there for a moment, grinned, and turned back into the police station.
Ilya Petrovitch had sat down and was rummaging through some papers. Before him stood the same peasant who had jostled past on the stairs.
"Back again! Leave something behind? What's the matter?"
Raskolnikov, his lips white and his eyes staring, walked slowly up to the desk, leaned his hand on it, and tried to speak. But no words came -- only incoherent sounds.
"You're feeling ill! A chair! Here, sit down! Water!"
Raskolnikov collapsed into the chair, but kept his eyes fixed on the face of Ilya Petrovitch, which now showed unpleasant surprise. They stared at each other for a full minute. Someone brought water.
"It was I..." Raskolnikov began.
"Drink some water."
Raskolnikov pushed the water away with his hand and, softly, haltingly, but distinctly, said:
"It was I who killed the old pawnbroker woman and her sister Lizaveta with an axe, and robbed them."
Ilya Petrovitch's mouth fell open. People came running from all directions.
Raskolnikov repeated his statement.
